decision.location: Introduction, p. 368, lines 56-60 (and Section I / I.A, pp. 371-375, Figure 2; References, p. 404)
decision.quote:
In reality, demand for
income redistribution in the United States has remained ﬂat by some mea-
sures and decreased according to others (see Kuziemko and others 2013),
as we document later in this paper.
decision.reason: Ashok, Kuziemko, and Washington (2015) cite Kuziemko et al. (2013, NBER WP 18865; linked as one report family in References, p. 404, to its revised 2015 American Economic Review article, 105(4): 1478–1508) for the flat/decreasing U.S. redistribution-demand trend (p. 368) and re-estimate it in Section I / I.A (pp. 371–375, Figure 2), distinct from shipped row 2155 (Kenworthy & McCall, 2007/2008). Both the 2013 NBER working paper (p. 1; Figure 1, p. 33) and the 2015 AER article (p. 1479, Figure 1) empirically plot historical GSS 8 - eqwlth responses since 1978, separate from their mTurk experiments. However, visual inspection of both Figure 1s shows that 2013 NBER Figure 1 ends at 2010, whereas 2015 AER Figure 1 extends to 2012 with visibly different points and fits; neither version states endpoints, GSS weights, or exclusions in text, captions, or appendix. In Section I.A, Ashok et al. analyze GSS eqwlth (weighted by wtssall * oversamp, excluding spanint = 2) using a preferred pre-recession fit through 2006 (a subset of both originals' historical waves, framed on p. 371 as checking that patterns are not driven by data or coding differences) and a full-sample fit through 2012. Relative to 2013 NBER Figure 1 (ending 2010), the 2012 wave is new data (replication); relative to 2015 AER Figure 1 (ending 2012), no post-2012 wave is added (reproduction). Because contemporaneous 2015 publication and bibliography linkage do not establish analysis chronology or identical GSS observations/weights, record_type (replication vs. reproduction) remains genuinely version-specific ambiguous.
